description: We are a collaborative team of developers and space enthusiasts passionate about building clean, impactful web tools. For this hackathon, we’ve come together to tackle the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge to make lunar mission data accessible and exciting to explore. We value clear communication, fast prototyping, and having fun while building a working, polished project.
summary:
LANDERPRINT is a hardware-aware lunar landing site navigator built for NASA Space Apps 2026. It helps compare real south-polar candidate sites and 2027 UTC windows by asking a clearer question than “is the Sun up?”: at this place and date, can a spacecraft with a chosen body heading keep power, Earth pointing, and a preliminary deployment path workable together?
Users choose among seven Connecting Ridge Extension sites, two October 2027 periods, and equal-area solar and antenna hardware presets, then rotate the lander’s heading. Live checks show solar incidence and battery margin, whether Earth is geometrically visible inside the antenna beam or gimbal limits, and a preliminary slope and ramp screen from a 5 m DEM. A 2D horizon instrument and a 3D scene show the same engine results: Sun and Earth against terrain skylines built from NASA’s A305 local DEM nested with LOLA far-field topography, with ephemeris checked against JPL Horizons and NAIF SPICE.
This matters because a sunlit site can still fail for a real lander orientation. LANDERPRINT makes those tradeoffs visible and honest. Unknown stays unknown, hardware is labeled hypothetical, and the tool is a research prototype, not a certified landing decision.
details:
LANDERPRINT is a web app for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge “Lunar Landing Site Navigator.” It helps you compare real lunar south-pole sites, dates, and lander headings.

What it does. Many tools only ask if the Sun is up. LANDERPRINT asks a harder question: if the lander faces this way, can it still get power, see Earth with its antenna, and have a workable path off the lander? You pick a site, a 2027 time window, and a hardware preset. Then you turn the lander’s heading. The app shows which checks pass, fail, or stay unknown.

How it works. Behind the scenes, Python builds science data from NASA maps and space-time tables. The app uses NASA’s A305 5 m terrain for the local ground, LOLA maps for distant hills out to 300 km, and Sun and Earth directions from SPICE that we checked against JPL Horizons. In the browser, TypeScript engines run the power, antenna, and slope checks on that data. A simple 2D horizon view is the main screen. An optional 3D view shows the same results as a lander on the terrain. The pictures never invent a pass or fail. Only the engines do.

Why it helps. A bright site can still be a bad fit for a given lander facing. One heading may collect more sunlight but miss Earth. Another may keep the antenna but leave less battery. LANDERPRINT makes those tradeoffs easy to see. Hardware presets are labeled hypothetical, and missing data shows as unknown. This is a research and teaching tool, not a certified flight decision.

What we built with. React, TypeScript, and Vite for the app. Three.js for 3D. Python, NumPy, rasterio, and SpiceyPy for science prep. Vitest and pytest for tests. Hosted as a static site on Vercel. No real spacecraft hardware was built. The solar presets keep the same total cell area so layouts can be compared fairly.

What makes it creative. We treat lander heading as the main control that links power, communications, and deployment on the same real site and date, then show that story in both a fast 2D instrument and an inspectable 3D scene.

What we were careful about. Honest science sources and checks. Clear limits of a 5 m map (it cannot see small rocks). Equal-area hardware comparisons. Keyboard-friendly controls. Keeping 2D as the safe default. No claim of NASA endorsement.
